chunks: Supply voltage, power and thermals. The question: How does supply voltage impact power, performance, and thermals?
Supply voltage is the electrical push that powers a chip's transistors, its tiny switches.
A higher voltage makes transistors switch faster, so the chip can run at a higher clock speed. But it costs a lot of power, and that power turns into heat.
Power grows with the square of the voltage, so a small cut saves a lot. Go too low, though, and the chip becomes too slow, and its memory can stop working.
Imagine filling a tall barrel. The higher the level you fill to, the more water the barrel holds. Each liter also has to be lifted higher.
Both effects grow with the level, so the energy grows with the level squared.
A higher water level also pushes water through the pipes faster, which is why a higher voltage gives a faster chip. But the barrel only models the cost side.
It says nothing about the wear that high voltage causes over the years.
Frequency (blue) rises with voltage but flattens at the top and falls steeply below about 0. 7 volts. Power at fixed frequency (red dashed) is a parabola.
Power when the chip is also run at the frequency the voltage allows (orange) rises about as fast as V to the 3 around the reference point.
The gap between curves is what DVFS exploits. Drag V t up to 0. 45 volts: at 0. 7 volts the achievable frequency falls from about 71% to 60% of the 0.
9 volts value, so a high-threshold process loses much more speed from undervolting.
Supply voltage ( V ): the electrical push that powers the transistors. Threshold voltage ( V t ): the voltage a transistor needs before it turns on.
Dynamic power: switching power, alpha C V squared f . Leakage: current that flows through transistors that are supposed to be off.
DVFS: changing voltage and frequency together to match the load. Guardband: extra voltage added on top of the minimum, to cover brief dips (droop), aging and variation.
A chip runs at 0. 9 volts and 2 gigahertz and uses 32. 4 watts. Cut the voltage 20%, to 0. 72 volts. At the same frequency, power falls to 0. 8 squared equals 0.
64 of the original, a 36% saving. But with a threshold of 0. 35 volts, the transistors are now slower, and the top clock drops to about 1. 49 gigahertz.
At that clock, power is about 15. 5 watts, roughly half. That is the whole idea.
"Dynamic power goes as V squared, so a 20% voltage cut saves 36% of dynamic power, and leakage falls even faster.

Performance also depends on voltage: drive current scales with V minus Vt, so delay shrinks and maximum frequency rises with voltage, with diminishing returns at high V and a steep slowdown near threshold.
Less power means less heat.
So voltage is the most effective power knob, limited below by SRAM and timing and above by reliability, which is why DVFS pairs voltage with frequency."
